newsitem.title: USA: GM braces for plant shutdowns due to parts strike.
newsitem.headline: GM braces for plant shutdowns due to parts strike.

text.p: General Motors Corp. planned to idle one assembly plant and was bracing for more shutdowns Thursday after workers struck a key transmission and wheel plant on Wednesday in the sixth walkout against the automaker this year.

GM spokesman Tom Klipstine said the strike at the GM Powertrain Division plant in Warren, Mich., would force the nation's largest automaker to idle 2,700 workers at its Buick City plant in Flint, Mich., starting Thursday.
"Everthing will run through today. However, Buick City employess are being told not to come in tomorrow," Klipstine said.

Buick City produces GM's large Buick LeSabre and Pontiac Bonneville sedans, which are equipped with the four-speed, front-drive automatic transmissions built at the strikebound Warren plant. A sister large-car plant in Orion Township, Mich., is expected to shut down later Thursday.

The roughly 2,800 hourly workers at the Warren plant walked off their jobs after a strike deadline expired at 11:59 p.m. EDT Tuesday. A second strike at a tail-light plant in Anderson, Ind., was narrowly averted when bargainers for GM and the United Auto Workers reached a tentative deal for a new local contract.

Hardly a week has gone by this year when GM has not dealt with a strike or a strike threat over jobs and out-sourcing. The automaker, seeking to shrink its workforce through normal attrition to better compete with domestic and Japanese rivals, has been locked in an epic battle with the UAW over staffing levels.

Workers at the Warren plant in suburban Detroit complain that the workload for their shrinking staff has become so overwhelming that they cannot take time off and have difficulty taking restroom breaks.

"GM has gotten to the place where they no longer care about us and we have to stand up," said worker Jackie Kelly. "No one wants to strike. We don't want to hurt the company, We don't want ourselves, but we must stand together."
Talks continued at the Warren plant, but union officials reported little progress. A prolonged strike could force a number of GM car and truck assembly plants to shut down.

At risk are GM's new minivans and mid-size and large cars, including the new Pontiac Grand Prix, Oldsmobile Intrigue and Chevrolet Malibu sedans -- new models that are critical to GM's drive to regain market share this year.

Klipstine said minivan production in the Atlanta suburb of Doraville, Ga., could continue into next week, partly because it receives transmission shipments in larger batches than do GM's Michigan assembly plants.

In Anderson, Ind., GM reached a tentative local labour agreement with UAW Local 663, preventing a strike at GM's Delphi Interior and Lighting Systems plant, which makes tail lamps and other lighting products for nearly every GM vehicle built in North America.
A 1994 strike at the plant forced GM to idle 15 assembly plants and 50,000 workers in less than three days.
Local 663 officials said they expected the plant's 2,500 workers to vote on the contract deal next week.

"Did we get all we wanted? No, neither side got everything, but that's negotitations," said Local 663 President Ollie Dixon. "I do feel we achieved an agreement that the membership can live with. It addresssed the key issue of job security."
The Warren strike comes less than a week after GM settled one of the longest strikes in its history, a nearly three-month walkout at its Pontiac, Mich., pickup truck plant.
Workers at that plant, who lost as much as $15,000 each in wages during the strike, could be idled again, because the Warren plant makes some suspension control arms for GM trucks.
As part of the new accord, GM agreed to add 557 new production and skilled trades workers and pay a total of $9.5 million to settle grievances and cover missed holiday pay.
During the second quarter, the Pontiac strike and another walkout in Oklahoma City, shrank GM's profits by $490 million.
GM's stock rose $1.25 to $59 on the New York Stock Exchange.
